ERP Scheduling System

Architecture & Functionality Overview  |  September 2026

1. About ERP Scheduling System

ERP Scheduling System is built for STEM education centers that offer in-depth study of specific subjects (physics and/or chemistry) to students from multiple schools. Centers like this face a specific scheduling challenge — class days and times need to be coordinated across every partner school contributing students to a group. The application makes it easier for different staff roles — administrators, teachers, lab assistants — to manage dozens of operational workflows: from partner-school coordination to assigning labs and classrooms based on equipment ordered by teachers. It gives center management the ability to manage teacher workload (total working hours, teaching hours, group sizes) and make a variety of operational decisions. The system also collects, processes, and analyzes all statistical data related to the center's operations.

For centers like this, the schedule is never static. It changes daily — reschedules, substitutions, cancellations. The core job of Scheduling System is to make managing the center's schedule and resources transparent, intuitive, and easy to work with.
Key Capabilities
Technical Guarantees
Immutable data

2. Who Uses the System

The system has eight roles. A staff member can be assigned more than one role at a time.

Role Who They Are What They Do
Super Admin Technical lead Full access. Manages reference data, staff, and global settings.
Admin Any staff member with admin rights — including as a secondary role Reviews incoming schedule-change requests, clarifies details, and approves them. The only role that actually applies changes to the data — approve or reject.
Teacher Instructor Initiates schedule changes: reschedules, cancellations, substitutions, equipment orders. Everything goes through a request to the admin — teachers never edit data directly.
Lab Assistant Lab staff member Sees the list of upcoming lessons with ordered equipment. Prepares and delivers kits. Never creates or edits orders — only fulfills them.
Principal Center principal Full read access to the schedule and reports for any period. Manages teacher workload and assigns substitutes. Can also teach lessons (if also assigned as a teacher).
Vice Principal Deputy principal for academics Read access to the schedule and reports for teachers in their subject. Manages teacher workload and assigns substitutes. Can also teach lessons (if also assigned as a teacher).
Secretary Secretary / office administrator Read-only: full schedule, all reports, any period. Cannot make changes.
Center Coordinator Center staff member Handles school communication on behalf of the center. Supports partner schools, coordinates logistics.
Access rights are configured granularly — not just per role as a whole, but per individual action on specific screens (for example, "open a day for editing" or "assign a substitute teacher" can be granted to the principal and vice principal separately from full admin access). This allows precise, low-risk expansion of permissions.

3. Core Processes

3.1 Annual Template & Propagation

The schedule has two levels. The upper level is the annual weekly template: each teacher's and group's standard workload. The lower level is the actual week-by-week schedule for the whole academic year, generated from that template.

1Admin edits the template — reassigns the teacher, time, or day of a template slot.
2The system propagates the change — within seconds, updates only the weeks and slots affected: changed ones are updated, new ones are added, cancelled ones are removed. The whole schedule is never rebuilt from scratch.
3Existing work isn't lost — anything already accumulated around lessons the propagation didn't touch — equipment orders, comments, teacher requests — stays exactly as it was.
A lesson's room isn't picked arbitrarily — it's matched to actual need: fume hood, sink, blackout capability, or equipment already ordered.

3.2 Schedule Changes

The schedule is built for the academic year, but day-to-day adjustments come up constantly. The system routes them through a clear path:

1Teacher submits a request — specifies exactly what needs to change: reschedule a lesson, cancel it, adjust an equipment order, or change the room. Principals and vice principals, when they also teach, use the same system as regular teachers.
2The system checks for conflicts — at submission time, shows whether the room or teacher is already booked for that slot. The teacher sees a warning and can adjust the request or submit it anyway with the conflict flagged — the admin then resolves it manually.
3Admin reviews the request — sees the queue of incoming requests, adjusts details with the teacher if needed, and approves the change.
4The schedule updates — after every approved change, the schedule updates immediately and everyone sees the current state right away.
5The lesson is completed — the system marks it complete automatically once the lesson's end time passes.
The full change history is kept automatically — the admin can always see what the schedule looked like before a change and who made it.

3.3 Equipment Preparation

1Teacher adds equipment to a lesson request — when submitting a request for a new or modified lesson, selects the needed experiment from the catalog and the number of kits: for a demo or for hands-on student work. The whole request — lesson and equipment — goes to the admin together.
2Admin approves the request — reviews the lesson and equipment together and makes one decision. Once approved, the equipment order is automatically linked to the lesson.
3Lab assistant sees a daily summary — their interface shows upcoming orders: what to prepare, how many kits, for which class, and which room.
4Lab assistant assembles and delivers the equipment — puts together kits for each lesson based on the system's data.
5The order closes automatically after the lesson — the system marks it complete once the lesson ends.
Physical inventory tracking and automatic component reservation are planned as a separate module for a later stage.

3.4 Substitute Teachers

If a teacher can't take a lesson, the admin, principal, or vice principal picks a substitute from the list of teachers available at that time with a matching subject profile. The lesson immediately shows as a substitution everywhere — in the schedule and on the corridor displays.

The candidate list is generated automatically — the system only shows teachers who, at the same time, are: working at the center on that day and hour (based on the teacher's work schedule), qualified to teach the subject at that grade level, and not already booked for another lesson.
If no suitable substitute is available, a cancellation request for the lesson is created automatically for the admin.

3.5 Populating the System (Data Workflow)

Data is entered in a strict order — each step depends on the one before it.

Tables 1–6 — global data needed to build the tables and schedule that follow:

  1. subjects — subjects
  2. lesson_types — activity types
  3. equipment_physics — physics experiment catalog
  4. schools — partner schools
  5. staff — personnel
  6. rooms — rooms

Tables 7–9 — assigning students to groups:

  1. school_enrollment — how many students each school sends, by subject, lesson type, and grade (PK: school+subject+lesson_type; is_subset_of_regular for enriched programs)
  2. student_groups — group breakdown (max N students, set when the group is formed)
  3. group_schools — how many students from each school are in each group (student_count)

Table 10 — building slots (group + day + time + teacher) and creating the base template version:

  1. basic_schedule

Table 11 — calendar of non-working periods: holidays, vacations, emergencies. Filled in manually by the admin once a year:

  1. holidays_and_vacations

Table 12 — based on the template (table 10), the schedule for the full academic year is generated via generate_year_schedule(). Rooms are assigned automatically by subject priority. Over the course of the year, lessons can be cancelled, rescheduled, or moved online. Every lesson is self-contained: it stores lesson_date, day_of_week, week_number, academic_year — academic weeks are computed dynamically from these fields, with no separate table needed:

  1. lessons
All table IDs are fixed and never change on reinstall or restore from backup. This guarantees that every reference between tables stays valid at every stage.

4. What the System Is Made Of

The system is built from several independent components, each responsible for its own part:

Component What It Does
Database Stores all data and enforces every rule: validation, locking, change history
API server Accepts requests, checks who's allowed to do what, and passes commands to the database
Web interface Scheduling System, fully in Hebrew (RTL)
Corridor displays Dedicated screens for the center's hallways — the day's live schedule for teachers, and a simplified version for students, with no personal login (authenticated via a static device key)
Notifications An internal event queue (request submitted/approved/rejected) — currently shown inside the interface. Email and messenger notifications (Telegram, WhatsApp) are planned for later stages.
Infrastructure Deployed in Docker containers on an AWS server, with automatic daily database backups

5. Reliability & Security

  • Every user gets an access token after logging in. The token is valid for 2 hours (auto-logout after 20 minutes of inactivity) and carries their role. No valid token, no access — no exceptions.
  • Every rule is enforced at the database level — there's no way to bypass them through the interface.
  • The change history can't be altered or deleted — by any user, in any role. This guarantees full transparency for every action in the system.
  • The system automatically blocks scheduling conflicts.
  • Internet access is architected on a Zero Trust basis — via Cloudflare Tunnel.
